paragraphs: This paper develops a theoretical explanation of CasDF, a forest representation learning approach. It describes CasDF as an additive model whose successive contributions improve augmented features. This shifts the analysis toward the representations built across layers, rather than treating boosting solely as a way to improve the final prediction.

The central result connects generalization to the distribution of classification margins. The quantity of interest is the margin standard deviation divided by the margin mean: a measure of how spread out margins are relative to their average. When this ratio is sufficiently small, the authors improve the generalization-gap upper bound from order sqrt(ln m/m) to order ln m/m. The stronger bound therefore depends on a stated condition.

That analysis motivates a reweighting method designed to reduce the margin ratio while boosting augmented features. Experiments support a correlation between margin distributions and generalization performance. Together, the theory and method provide a way to guide layer-by-layer forest representation learning using a quantity tied to the bound.
neurips-2019-a-refined-margin-distributi.tldr: A conditional generalization bound motivates reweighting deep-forest training to reduce margin variability relative to the mean.

paragraphs: The paper asks how a neural system could learn visual motion from data while using biologically plausible learning rules. The underlying problem is to recognize transformations independently of image content: motion should be recognizable across different things being viewed. Consecutive video frames provide one setting for learning this capability without supervision.

The authors retain an approach that represents small transformations through transformation operators, but change the learning objective. Earlier work learned these operators by reducing image reconstruction error, which was difficult to translate into a plausible biological network. Here, an objective that preserves similarities leads to an online optimization algorithm that maps naturally onto a neural network with biologically plausible learning rules.

After training, the network reproduces major features of the fly's motion-detection circuit. In particular, its local detectors combine information from at least three neighboring pixels, consistent with experimental observations that conflict with the Hassenstein-Reichardt model. The result connects a learning objective to observed circuit organization without claiming a complete account of biological motion vision.
neurips-2019-a-similarity-preserving-net.tldr: A similarity-preserving learning objective produces a biologically plausible motion network that reproduces key features of the fly motion detector.

paragraphs: This paper targets the parameter demands of multi-head attention in Transformers. Although self-attention has enabled strong language-processing models, the authors identify its multi-head implementation as an obstacle to deployment with limited resources. Their aim is to make the attention component more compact while retaining its usefulness for language modeling and translation.

The proposed replacement, Multi-linear attention, combines parameter sharing with Block-Term Tensor Decomposition. The key idea is to express the attention model through a structured decomposition, allowing parameters to be shared within that representation. Compression is therefore built into the attention mechanism itself, making the design a different parameterization of how the model handles attention.

The authors evaluate the method on PTB, WikiText-103, and One-billion language modeling tasks, together with WMT-2016 English-German translation. They report substantial parameter compression and performance improvements relative to several language modeling approaches, including Transformer, Transformer-XL, and a Transformer using tensor train decomposition. These findings show that the proposed structure can reduce parameter requirements while improving measured performance in the reported evaluations.
neurips-2019-a-tensorized-transformer-fo.tldr: Multi-linear attention uses tensor decomposition and parameter sharing to compress Transformers while improving performance in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a way to train deep Markov random fields, which are undirected graphical models. Its starting point is the difficulty of handling the partition function that normalizes such a model. The authors construct a training objective from a Bethe free energy approximation to this quantity, giving a tractable route to learning expressive models.

The resulting objective is a saddle-point problem and differs from an evidence lower bound, or ELBO. The authors can calculate exact gradients of this derived objective, and its computation requires no sampling. Exact gradients here refer to the chosen objective; the partition function still enters through an approximation. Trained inference networks amortize the optimization, allowing learned inference to support the overall procedure.

Experiments find favorable results against loopy belief propagation while requiring less time. The approach also achieves better held-out log likelihood than other recent approximate inference schemes considered. The contribution combines a computationally manageable objective with reusable learned inference, supporting both efficient training and favorable predictive fit in the reported comparisons.
neurips-2019-amortized-bethe-free-energy.tldr: A sampling-free Bethe-based objective and learned inference networks enable efficient MRF training with favorable held-out likelihood results.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a weakness of conventional convolutional neural networks: recognizing objects across changes in three-dimensional viewpoint. Strong performance on other tasks does not automatically supply this capability. The authors investigate whether a design inspired by binocular vision can improve viewpoint generalization while remaining compatible with the broader family of CNN-based techniques.

Their model, CNN², receives two images, resembling the paired views supplied by a left and right eye. It introduces augmentation, pooling, and convolutional layers intended to develop a sense of three-dimensionality recursively. The paired input and the modified processing layers work together as the architectural proposal; the approach retains a convolutional foundation that can fit existing application-specific methods.

Empirical evaluation finds better viewpoint generalization than vanilla CNNs. The authors also describe the model as straightforward to implement and train, with compatibility across specialized CNN techniques. These findings support binocular input as a useful design direction for the evaluated settings, without establishing that the model reaches the viewpoint understanding of human vision.
neurips-2019-cnn-2-viewpoint-generalizat.tldr: CNN² processes paired images with modified convolutional components to improve viewpoint generalization over vanilla CNNs.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to test whether variables remain dependent after conditioning on other information, with particular attention to high-dimensional features. The goal is a statistical decision about conditional dependence. The authors approach this by learning a distribution that represents the null hypothesis, giving the test a data-driven reference for what conditional independence would look like.

A generative adversarial network directly approximates the relevant conditional distribution. Samples from that network enter a new test statistic designed to improve statistical power. The stated guarantee for controlling false positives depends on density approximation being viable. Under that requirement, the approach does not need assumptions specifying the form of the distributions or the dependencies among features.

Synthetic experiments with high-dimensional data show significant power gains over competing methods. The authors also illustrate the test's use in discovering causal disease markers from genetic data. These results connect flexible conditional modeling to hypothesis testing, while the theoretical claim retains its dependence on the ability to approximate the required density.
neurips-2019-conditional-independence-te.tldr: A GAN-based conditional-independence test improves power in high-dimensional simulations and controls false positives when the required density approximation is viable.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how batch size and learning rate should be considered together when training neural networks with stochastic gradient descent. Its proposed strategy is to keep the ratio of batch size to learning rate from becoming too large. This frames the two hyperparameters as a coupled choice relevant to performance on unseen data.

The theoretical contribution is a PAC-Bayes generalization bound that is positively correlated with this ratio. A larger ratio is associated with a larger bound, providing a mathematical basis for the proposed training strategy. This is a statement about the bound, rather than a guarantee that every individual model's test performance changes monotonically with the ratio.

The empirical study trains 1,600 models using ResNet-110 and VGG-19 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 while controlling unrelated variables. Analysis across 164 groups uses Spearman rank correlations and associated p values, finding statistically significant relationships that support the strategy. Together, the evidence motivates tuning batch size relative to learning rate when seeking good generalization.
neurips-2019-control-batch-size-and-lear.tldr: A generalization bound and controlled experiments support keeping the batch-size-to-learning-rate ratio from becoming too large.

paragraphs: This paper treats safe reinforcement learning as policy optimization subject to a constraint. With nonlinear function approximation, both the objective and the constraint can be nonconvex, making the optimization problem difficult. The aim is to develop an update procedure with a convergence result for this constrained setting.

The method builds a sequence of simpler optimization problems. At each stage, local convex quadratic functions replace the original nonconvex functions, using information obtained from policy gradient estimators. Each surrogate problem retains a constrained form, so the procedure addresses the objective and constraint together while working with local approximations that are more manageable to optimize.

The authors prove that solutions of these surrogate problems converge to a stationary point of the original problem. Stationarity is the stated guarantee; the abstract does not claim a globally optimal policy. They also apply the algorithm to optimal control and multi-agent reinforcement learning examples with safety constraints, extending the presentation from a convergence argument to concrete constrained decision-making settings.
neurips-2019-convergent-policy-optimizat.tldr: Local convex quadratic surrogate problems yield a policy optimization method with convergence to a stationary point of the original safety-constrained problem.

paragraphs: Time series can be difficult to compare when corresponding events occur at different times or unfold at different speeds. The paper addresses this nonlinear timing variation through joint alignment. Traditional methods align a particular collection but require a new optimization problem for unseen signals; multi-class methods also require classification before alignment.

Diffeomorphic Temporal Alignment Nets learn an input-dependent nonlinear time transformation through temporal transformer layers. After training, the network aligns a new signal with a forward pass. This turns alignment into a learned mapping that can be reused, allowing the cost of learning an alignment rule to support later processing of previously unseen data.

The supervision requirements depend on the setting. Single-class training uses no known ground-truth alignments. Multi-class training uses class labels but still does not require ground-truth alignments, and class labels are unavailable at test time. The reported results show stronger training-data alignment than existing joint-alignment methods and good generalization to test signals, supporting the usefulness of learning a reusable alignment procedure.
neurips-2019-diffeomorphic-temporal-alig.tldr: DTAN learns signal-dependent time warps that align unseen time series through a forward pass without requiring ground-truth alignments.

paragraphs: This paper studies choosing the best option in a multi-armed bandit problem when both expected reward and risk matter. The target combines expected reward with Conditional Value at Risk, or CVaR, through a linear objective. The learner receives a fixed sampling budget and must identify the option that optimizes this criterion.

The proposed algorithms do not require advance information about reward distributions, including bounds on moments or tails, or gaps between options. The setting allows unbounded and even heavy-tailed rewards. To support this goal, the authors develop a CVaR estimator for such random variables and prove a concentration inequality, then establish upper bounds on the probability of selecting the wrong option.

The paper compares these bounds with those for algorithms that do use distributional information. Numerical experiments find competitive performance, suggesting that dispensing with this prior information need not impose a substantial practical penalty in the tested settings. The contribution joins risk-sensitive selection with guarantees for algorithms that operate without the specified distributional knowledge.
neurips-2019-distribution-oblivious-risk.tldr: Risk-aware best-arm algorithms handle unbounded rewards without prior distributional information and provide bounds on incorrect selection.

paragraphs: The paper tackles a data problem in developing Boolean satisfiability solvers: real-world benchmark formulas are limited, yet empirical testing is central to solver development. Handcrafted synthetic generators can expand the available collection, but the authors argue that existing approaches do not simultaneously reproduce the broad range of characteristics found in real instances.

G2SAT learns to generate formulas from a supplied set of examples. Its central representation converts SAT formulas into latent bipartite graphs, which a specialized deep generative neural network models. This lets the generation process learn structural patterns from the input formulas, providing a way to build synthetic examples around characteristics of an existing benchmark collection.

The generated formulas resemble real-world instances according to both graph measurements and SAT solver behavior. These two assessments connect structural similarity with how solvers respond to the formulas. The authors further show that the synthetic formulas could improve solver performance on real-world benchmarks, supporting learned generation as a useful tool for solver development and investigation.
neurips-2019-g2sat-learning-to-generate-.tldr: G2SAT learns graph-based SAT formula generation, producing instances that resemble real benchmarks and could help improve solver performance.

paragraphs: The paper examines neural networks before training, when randomly chosen weights and biases define a collection of possible models. These initialization choices affect how trainable individual networks are and how quickly training proceeds. Understanding this starting distribution can therefore reveal properties of the models from which learning selects a solution.

Earlier analyses use mean-field approximations that assume infinitely wide layers and examine average squared signals. The authors instead derive the exact joint distribution of signal outputs for fully connected networks with Gaussian weights and biases. This allows them to analyze departures from mean-field predictions while retaining information about the output distribution beyond an average squared quantity.

For ReLU networks, the paper then examines shortcomings of the standard initialization, including its failure to provide dynamical isometry. The proposed alternative uses parameter sharing at initialization to overcome these limitations. The contribution links a more exact description of random networks to an initialization design, under the stated fully connected Gaussian setting for the distributional analysis.
neurips-2019-initialization-of-relus-for.tldr: An exact analysis of Gaussian-initialized networks motivates initial parameter sharing to address standard ReLU initialization's lack of dynamical isometry.

paragraphs: This paper studies semantic segmentation when training information comes from several synthetic sources with different distributions and must transfer to real images. A method designed around one source does not readily resolve differences among multiple sources. The proposed Multi-source Adversarial Domain Aggregation Network, or MADAN, addresses these differences within an end-to-end framework.

MADAN first produces an adapted domain for each source. It aligns images toward the target at the pixel level using cycle consistency, while maintaining dynamic semantic consistency. Two discriminator components then encourage the adapted domains to come closer together. Finally, the framework aligns features between the aggregated domain and the target while training the segmentation network.

This sequence addresses source-to-target differences and differences among the sources themselves. Experiments transfer from synthetic GTA and SYNTHIA data to real Cityscapes and BDDS data, with reported performance exceeding state-of-the-art approaches. The results support combining image adaptation, source aggregation, and feature alignment for the evaluated multi-source segmentation transfers.
neurips-2019-multi-source-domain-adaptat.tldr: MADAN combines pixel adaptation, source-domain aggregation, and feature alignment to improve semantic segmentation transfer from multiple synthetic sources.

paragraphs: Multilabel classification allows each example to have several relevant labels. A common training strategy reduces the task to binary or multiclass problems, but the resulting loss may favor a particular evaluation measure. This paper asks how five common reductions relate to precision at k and recall at k.

The analysis includes one-versus-all and multiclass reductions, along with normalized variants that scale each example's contribution by its number of relevant labels. The authors identify the risks underlying these objectives and prove that each reduction is consistent with either precision or recall. This gives a formal interpretation of what the training loss is aligned to optimize.

A further result shows that, in general, a reduction cannot be optimal for both measures. Consequently, choosing a loss involves the intended evaluation criterion, not just a convenient way to organize training. Experiments support the analysis by demonstrating cases where normalized reductions improve recall over unnormalized alternatives. Those gains are scenario-dependent, consistent with the paper's distinction between the two objectives.
neurips-2019-multilabel-reductions-what-.tldr: Five common multilabel reductions align with either precision or recall, and no reduction is generally optimal for both.

paragraphs: The paper investigates what convolutional networks can achieve when their width grows without limit. Neural tangent kernels offer a way to study this regime through kernel methods, connecting trained neural networks with a more directly analyzable predictor. The practical challenge is computing the convolutional version of this kernel efficiently and exactly.

The authors provide an exact algorithm for the Convolutional Neural Tangent Kernel, or CNTK, together with an efficient GPU implementation. On CIFAR-10, the resulting pure kernel method sets a new reported performance benchmark. The abstract describes performance as 10% higher than the cited earlier methods and 6% lower than the corresponding finite network after batch normalization and related components are disabled.

The paper also establishes a non-asymptotic equivalence result: a fully trained, sufficiently wide network matches the kernel regression predictor using NTK. The width qualification matters to this claim. Together, the computation and proof make the infinite-width perspective useful for both concrete classification comparisons and theoretical understanding of trained networks.
neurips-2019-on-exact-computation-with-a.tldr: An efficient exact convolutional neural tangent kernel algorithm enables strong kernel classification results alongside a sufficiently-wide-network equivalence proof.

paragraphs: The paper introduces data for studying representations that separate meaningful factors such as object color, shape, size, and position. Much disentanglement research relies on synthetic toy datasets because collecting real observations is expensive. The authors create a controlled physical setting that allows the relationship between simulation and real-world representation learning to be examined systematically.

Their dataset contains more than one million images of physical three-dimensional objects with seven factors of variation. A robotic arm moves the objects so that the factors can be controlled precisely. Two additional datasets simulate the experimental setup, providing corresponding settings in which methods can be assessed on synthetic and real observations.

An initial study finds that learned models transfer poorly, while model and hyperparameter selection provide an effective way to transfer information to the real world. This distinguishes transferring a trained representation from transferring choices about how representations should be learned. The datasets make it possible to investigate both routes under controlled variation.
neurips-2019-on-the-transfer-of-inductiv.tldr: Controlled real and simulated object datasets show poor direct model transfer but useful transfer through model and hyperparameter selection.

paragraphs: PowerSGD addresses communication costs in data-parallel training, where workers need to combine gradient information. Reducing the amount of communicated data can help, but compression must also be fast and preserve test performance. The paper focuses on meeting these requirements together so that compression translates into shorter actual training time.

The proposed method represents gradients through a low-rank compressor. Its design supports rapid compression and efficient aggregation using all-reduce, the collective communication operation used to combine information across workers. Compatibility with this aggregation mechanism matters because a compact representation is useful only if the distributed system can combine it efficiently.

In the reported evaluations, PowerSGD achieves test performance comparable to SGD and reduces training times for convolutional networks and LSTMs on common datasets. It is the only evaluated compression method to deliver consistent wall-clock speedups against regular SGD using an optimized communication backend. This comparison supports a practical efficiency claim within the tested methods and workloads, rather than merely a reduction in communication volume.
neurips-2019-powersgd-practical-low-rank.tldr: PowerSGD combines fast low-rank gradient compression with efficient all-reduce to shorten tested training runs while matching SGD's test performance.

paragraphs: This paper develops representations for entities and relations in knowledge graphs using quaternions. A quaternion has one real component and three imaginary components, providing a richer representation than a complex number. Entities receive quaternion embeddings, while relations act as rotations in this space, giving the model a geometric interpretation.

Interactions use the Hamilton product, which couples the components of the representations. The authors argue that this captures dependencies among all components while encouraging compact entity-relation interactions. Quaternion rotations also offer more degrees of freedom than rotations in the complex plane. The framework extends ComplEx into hypercomplex space and can represent symmetry, anti-symmetry, and inversion, three important patterns in relations.

The method achieves reported state-of-the-art results on four established knowledge graph completion benchmarks. These experiments support the usefulness of the representation for predicting missing graph relationships. The contribution combines expressive interactions with a geometric account of relations, rather than presenting additional representational dimensions without explaining how entities and relations interact.
neurips-2019-quaternion-knowledge-graph-.tldr: Quaternion entity embeddings and rotational relations capture rich relational patterns and achieve reported state-of-the-art knowledge graph completion results.

paragraphs: The paper asks how a trained recurrent neural network actually carries out sentiment classification. Its goal is a quantitative account of the computation inside the network, going beyond treating the hidden state as an opaque representation. The authors use dynamical systems tools to examine the behavior of trained recurrent models.

They locate fixed points of the recurrent dynamics and approximate the nonlinear system locally around those points with linear dynamics. The arrangement of the fixed points and their nearby behavior reveal an approximate line attractor. This provides a low-dimensional structure through which the authors can explain how the network solves sentiment classification, despite its capacity for much more complicated high-dimensional computations.

The mechanism appears across LSTMs, GRUs, and vanilla RNNs trained on multiple datasets. This breadth suggests that the observed computation is not peculiar to a single architecture or dataset. The finding supports the possibility of shared, interpretable mechanisms across recurrent networks, while the line-attractor description remains approximate and tied to the studied sentiment tasks.
neurips-2019-reverse-engineering-recurre.tldr: Dynamical systems analysis reveals an approximate line attractor that explains sentiment computation across several recurrent architectures and datasets.

paragraphs: This paper studies finite-sample expressivity: how large a ReLU network must be to fit a collection of data points perfectly. It shows how depth can reduce the number of hidden nodes needed for memorization. For three-layer networks, the authors construct networks with square-root-in-N hidden-node scaling that memorize most datasets containing N points.

The analysis gives matching necessary and sufficient width scaling of order sqrt(N) for its memorization result. It also extends the construction to deeper networks, where a number of hidden-layer parameters scaling at least linearly with N is sufficient. Combined with an existing VC-dimension upper bound, the construction is nearly tight when depth is fixed.

The authors separately study residual networks under a general-position assumption, substantially reducing earlier hidden-node requirements. They also analyze SGD near a memorizing global minimum, showing that such an initialization quickly leads to a nearby point with much lower empirical risk. This optimization result is local: its stated starting condition is proximity to a memorizing minimum.
neurips-2019-small-relu-networks-are-pow.tldr: Depth enables compact ReLU networks to memorize many samples, with tight width bounds and a local SGD result near memorizing minima.

paragraphs: Spectral clustering uses information from a graph's eigenvalues to approximate difficult partitioning objectives based on conductance. The paper focuses on a source of poor approximations: the gap between conductance and the second eigenvalue. It asks whether changing the graph's spectral properties while preserving its cuts can make spectral clustering more effective.

The theoretical result states that every graph has a cut-similar counterpart called a spectral maximizer. This counterpart has eigenvalues close to the theoretical limit permitted by the original graph's cut structure. Spectral clustering on it therefore has the potential to find improved cuts that remain relevant to the original graph because the two graphs have similar cuts.

The authors then describe a practical modification algorithm that raises eigenvalues while preserving cuts. Combining this transformation with spectral clustering produces demonstrated improvements in the resulting cuts. The existence result motivates the approach, while the practical algorithm shows how altering the spectral representation can improve clustering without abandoning the partition structure of interest.
neurips-2019-spectral-modification-of-gr.tldr: Cut-preserving graph modification raises eigenvalues and yields improved cuts when followed by spectral clustering.

paragraphs: This paper studies faster hierarchical clustering for high-dimensional Euclidean data. It considers average linkage, single linkage, and Ward's method, which repeatedly merge clusters according to different notions of closeness. Exact implementations encounter the difficulty of finding closest pairs, motivating the question of how much speed approximation can provide.

The relaxation permits a merge whose criterion is at most gamma times the best currently available value. The authors show that the approximate clustering tree can be built with a nearly linear number of gamma-approximate nearest-neighbor queries. Their resulting runtime is approximately nd, up to logarithmic factors, plus n raised to 1 + O(1/gamma), where n counts points and d is dimension.

The result makes the approximation parameter part of the computational tradeoff while covering three widely used merging rules. Experiments show classification performance comparable to the exact versions alongside significant speedups. Thus, the paper offers both a theoretical route to faster clustering and empirical evidence that approximate merges can retain downstream usefulness in the tested tasks.
neurips-2019-subquadratic-high-dimension.tldr: Allowing approximately closest merges enables faster high-dimensional hierarchical clustering with comparable classification performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Functional Neural Processes model distributions over functions through relationships among data points. The authors introduce them as a family of exchangeable stochastic processes. Their central mechanism learns a graph of dependencies over latent representations of the observed points, making relational structure the basis for the model's account of function uncertainty.

This produces a Bayesian model without explicitly specifying a prior over global latent parameters. Instead, the prior concerns the dataset's relational structure, which the authors describe as easier to formulate. The paper explains how to learn the model with mini-batch optimization, allowing it to scale to large datasets, and how to predict at new points through a posterior predictive distribution.

Experiments cover toy regression and image classification. Compared with baselines that use global latent parameters, FNPs provide competitive predictions and more robust uncertainty estimates. The findings support relational modeling as an alternative way to build probabilistic function models, combining practical training with favorable uncertainty behavior in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2019-the-functional-neural-proce.tldr: Functional Neural Processes learn dependencies among data points to deliver competitive predictions and more robust uncertainty estimates than tested global-latent baselines.

paragraphs: The paper develops visual object representations for control and reinforcement learning. Its model, Transporter, represents objects through a small set of keypoints expressed as image coordinates. This gives the learner a concise geometric description, with the intended usefulness measured through tracking and action-oriented tasks.

Transporter learns from raw video frames without supervision. It moves learned image features between frames through a keypoint bottleneck, making the keypoints central to how the network relates observations over time. The discovered points track objects and object parts over long periods more accurately than the recent similar methods considered in the paper.

The resulting temporal consistency supports two control findings. Feeding keypoint coordinates and associated image features into reinforcement learning enables high sample efficiency. Learning to explore by controlling keypoint positions also sharply reduces the search space, reaching states that random-action exploration did not reach, without extrinsic rewards. These results connect an unsupervised geometric representation to both efficient learning and deeper exploration in the studied control domains.
neurips-2019-unsupervised-learning-of-ob.tldr: Transporter learns object keypoints from unlabeled video that support accurate tracking, sample-efficient reinforcement learning, and exploration without extrinsic rewards.

paragraphs: XLNet addresses a tradeoff in language-model pretraining. Masked approaches such as BERT learn from context on both sides of a position, but the paper identifies two drawbacks: neglected dependencies among masked positions and a mismatch between masked pretraining inputs and fine-tuning. The authors seek bidirectional context within an autoregressive formulation.

The method maximizes expected likelihood across permutations of the factorization order. Changing this order allows prediction to use different combinations of context while maintaining autoregressive modeling. The permutations concern the order in which the joint probability is factorized. XLNet also incorporates ideas from Transformer-XL into its pretraining design, combining that model's contributions with the new objective.

Under comparable experimental settings, XLNet outperforms BERT on 20 tasks, often by substantial margins. These include question answering, natural language inference, sentiment analysis, and document ranking. The results support the proposed combination across several forms of language understanding, while the comparison remains tied to the reported experimental conditions.
neurips-2019-xlnet-generalized-autoregre.tldr: XLNet learns bidirectional context through autoregressive factorization permutations and outperforms BERT on 20 tasks under comparable experimental settings.
